newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan cabinet shares shock over boy's murder.
newsitem.headline: Japan cabinet shares shock over boy's murder.

text.p: Japan's cabinet on Tuesday took up the murder and mutilation of a schoolboy by an older playmate, with ministers calling for curbs on media violence and echoing critics who say the nation is too lenient on juvenile crime.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called for "calm analysis" of the crime -- in which a 14-year-old boy admitted to slaying and beheading an 11-year-old boy in the central city of Kobe -- that has gripped Japan for weeks.
"Many issues will emerge from this case and I want it handled after a calm analysis of those matters," Hashimoto told reporters.
In an intense round of soul-searching spawned by the case, experts have blamed a breakdown of family values, a repressive education system and the proliferation of violent movies and video games.

The arrest of the self-confessed killer, whose name was not released because he is a minor, has cast a harsh light on Japan's high-pressure education system, as he said he killed his 11-year-old acquaintance "because he felt resentment against the school he has been going to", prosecutors said.
Farm Minister Takao Fujimoto said "problems of the education system" were behind the May 24 killing of Jun Hase, 11.

The boy's severed head was found at the gate of the junior high school attended by the suspect in Kobe on May 27, three days after he went missing. A note stuck in his mouth said the murderer was taking revenge against the education system.
"It is important to educate children well until they grow up so that they can tell right from wrong," Fujimoto said.
In response to revelations that the young killer was inspired by violent videos and "manga" comic books, two cabinet ministers said the government should try to curb media violence.

"Obscene films and videos are now restricted, but films without any literary or educational merit made just to show cruel scenes can easily be watched by adolescents," Construction Minister Shizuka Kamei told a news conference.

Cabinet spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said he thought the case would prompt public opinion to call for a re-examination of Japan's Juvenile Act, in which offenders under 16 are tried in Family Courts and not criminal courts.
"We must determine how to deal with youths who commit crimes fully aware that they will not face criminal punishment," Kajiyama told a news conference.
If convicted, the 14-year-old suspect would face a maximum sentence of just two years at a juvenile correction centre for the killing.
Crimes by junior high school students, aged 13 to 15, have been growing at an alarming pace, according to police statistics, although the figures are still low compared with some Western countries.
Last year 36,787 junior high school students were arrested for serious crimes such as assault and murder, a rise of 27 percent over the previous year.
